etymology: Webster 1828 prints WILL as noun (faculty, choice, command, divine determination, testament) and as verb transitive (to determine, command, dispose by testament; also the auxiliary of the future). This page keeps two longer senses in one spelling: the decree and faculty, and the act of determining. Companion pages already treat providence, decree, and sovereignty.
biblical_def:
Will is one spelling with two honest senses. Do not mash them.

1. Decree, faculty, command. Will is that by which a person determines to do or forbear. In Scripture the first will is God's. The Son teaches us to pray, Your kingdom come. Your will be done on earth as it is in heaven. Creature will is real, but it is not a rival throne. A man reasons, judges, and then wills; he does not author the world by wishing.

2. To determine; to say what shall be. As a verb, will is to decide that something shall be done or forborne, and, in common English, the sign of the future. James cuts the boast: you ought to say, If the Lord wills, we shall live and do this or that. The dictionary therefore keeps will from becoming a mood board. God wills. Man answers. The future is not a self-issued promissory note.
webster_summary: Webster 1828: WILL, noun — the faculty by which we determine to do or forbear; choice; command; divine determination (Thy will be done); testament. WILL, verb transitive — to determine; to command; also the auxiliary of the future tense.
webster_full: WILL, noun [See the Verb.]
1. That faculty of the mind by which we determine either to do or forbear an action; the faculty which is exercised in deciding, among two or more objects, which we shall embrace or pursue.
4. Command; direction. Our prayers should be according to the will of God.
7. Divine determination; moral purpose or counsel. Thy will be done. Lords Prayer.
8. Testament; the disposition of a man's estate, to take effect after his death.
WILL, verb transitive
1. To determine; to decide in the mind that something shall be done or forborne; implying power to carry the purpose into effect. In this manner God wills whatever comes to pass.
7. will is used as an auxiliary verb, and a sign of the future tense. I will go, is a present promise to go; and with an emphasis on will it expresses determination.
scriptures: Matthew 6:10
Your kingdom come. Your will be done On earth as it is in heaven.
James 4:15
Instead you ought to say, “If the Lord wills, we shall live and do this or that.”
corruption_summary: Will is corrupted when the creature's preference is crowned as sacred, when 'live your truth' replaces 'Thy will be done,' and when tomorrow is planned as if the Lord had not spoken.
corruption_paragraphs: The first corruption is the sovereign self. Webster still knew will as a faculty under judgment, not a god. The age catechizes children to 'follow your will' as if desire were decree. Matthew 6:10 is the Son teaching us to ask that the Father's will be done, not that ours be ratified.

The second corruption is 'God's will' as a stamp on whatever a man already wanted. James 4:15 is not a slogan for branding. It is a rebuke of boast: If the Lord wills, we shall live. Therapy talk that treats will as authentic feeling, and prosperity talk that treats will as a lever, both refuse that sentence.
The third corruption is the future auxiliary cut loose from providence. 'I will' becomes self-creation. Scripture does not deny planning. It denies the lie that a man authors his days.

Plan under the clause: If the Lord wills, we shall live and do this or that (James 4:15).
Do not call a preference a decree, and do not call a decree a vibe.

etymology: Webster 1828 prints STILL as verb (to stop motion or noise; to calm), adjective (silent, quiet, motionless), noun (calm; also the distilling vessel), and adverb (to this time; nevertheless; always). This page keeps two longer senses in one spelling: quiet that stops, and 'yet / to this time.' The distilling vessel is a third spelling-share; it is not mashed into the biblical quiet. Companion pages already treat rest, wait, and peace.
biblical_def:
Still is one spelling with two honest senses. Do not mash them.

1. Quiet, stopped, not agitated. To still is to check motion or noise. To be still is to be silent, calm, motionless. Moses says to the people, Do not be afraid. Stand still, and see the salvation of the LORD. The psalm says, Be still, and know that I am God. This is not emptied mind. It is stopped panic under a God who will be exalted in the earth.

2. Yet; to this time; nevertheless. The adverb keeps a fact in force: it is still true; he is still afraid; they kept still the office. Scripture's quiet is not the same word as 'still going.' The dictionary therefore keeps still from becoming a spa verb. God stills, or you are only holding your breath.
webster_summary: Webster 1828: STILL, verb — to stop motion or noise; to calm. STILL, adjective — silent; quiet; motionless. STILL, adverb — to this time; nevertheless; always. A separate noun names the distilling vessel.
webster_full: STILL, verb transitive
1. To stop, as motion or agitation; to check or restrain; to make quiet; as, to still the raging sea.
2. To stop, as noise; to silence.
3. To appease; to calm; to quiet; as tumult, agitation or excitement; as, to still the passions.
STILL, adjective
1. Silent; uttering no sound.
3. Motionless; as, to stand still; to lie or sit still.
STILL, adverb
1. To this time; till now.
2. Nevertheless; notwithstanding.
STILL, noun [Latin , to drop. See Distill.] A vessel, boiler or copper used in the distillation of liquors.
scriptures: Psalm 46:10
Be still, and know that I am God; I will be exalted among the nations, I will be exalted in the earth!
Exodus 14:13

And Moses said to the people, “Do not be afraid. Stand still, and see the salvation of the LORD, which He will accomplish for you today. For the Egyptians whom you see today, you shall see again no more forever.
corruption_summary: Still is corrupted when 'be still' is recast as emptied-mind wellness, when standing still is mocked as passivity, and when the adverb 'still' is used to keep a sin in force as if time had baptized it.
corruption_paragraphs: The first corruption is mindfulness as Scripture. Psalm 46:10 is Be still, and know that I am God — not be still and know yourself. The age sells stillness as a nervous-system hack. The psalm sells the knowledge of God and His exaltation among the nations.
The second corruption is motion as virtue. Exodus 14:13 is Stand still, and see the salvation of the LORD. Hustle calls that weakness. Israel would have died in the water they tried to manage.
The third corruption is the adverb as excuse. 'We still do it this way' can be fidelity, or it can be unbelief with a calendar. Webster's nevertheless does not pardon what God has named sin.

usage: Be still, and know that I am God — knowledge, not vacancy (Psalm 46:10).
Stand still, and see the salvation of the LORD (Exodus 14:13).
Keep the quiet sense and the 'yet' sense apart; do not baptize a still with gin.

etymology: Webster 1828 prints PRES'ENT, adjective (Latin praesens: being in a place; now existing; ready at hand) and PRESENT', verb transitive (to set before a superior; to offer; to give; to lay before a court). The noun is that which is given. This page keeps two longer senses in one spelling: being here/now, and setting a thing or a body before the Lord. Companion pages already treat worship, sacrifice, and gift.
biblical_def:
Present is one spelling with two honest senses. Stress shifts with the sense. Do not mash them.

1. Being here; now existing; not absent. Present is opposed to absent, past, and future. Jesus says, These things I have spoken to you while being present with you. The disciples had His face then. The church has His Spirit now. 'The present' is not a shrine. It is the hour under God's eye.

2. To set before; to offer. To present is to place before a superior. There was a day when the sons of God came to present themselves before the LORD. Paul beseeches the brethren to present their bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable to God. A wrapped gift may be a present. Romans 12 is not Christmas. The dictionary therefore keeps present from becoming a mindfulness brand. You are present before God, or you are only nearby.
webster_summary: Webster 1828: PRES'ENT, adjective — being in a place; now existing; ready at hand (John 14:25). PRESENT', verb transitive — to set before a superior (Job 1:6); to offer; to give. PRESENT, noun — a gift.
webster_full: PRES'ENT, adjective s as z. [Latin praesens; prae and sum, esse, to be.]
1. Being in a certain place; opposed to absent.
2. Being before the face or near; being in company. These things have I spoken unto you, being yet present with you. John 14:25.
4. Now existing, or being at this time; not past or future.
PRESENT', verb transitive
1. To set, place or introduce into the presence or before the face of a superior. Now there was a day when the sons of God came to present themselves before the Lord. Job 1:6.
4. To give; to offer gratuitously for reception.
PRES'ENT, noun That which is presented or given; a gift; a donative.
scriptures: Romans 12:1
I beseech you therefore, brethren, by the mercies of God, that you present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable to God, which is your reasonable service.
John 14:25
These things I have spoken to you while being present with you.
corruption_summary: Present is corrupted when 'be present' is recast as mindfulness, when the living sacrifice is swapped for a lifestyle gift, and when 'living in the moment' is used to dodge judgment and hope.
corruption_paragraphs: The first corruption is the wellness slogan. 'Be present' in the age means notice your breath. John 14:25 is the Son present with His own, speaking words. Attention without the Lord is still absence from Him.

The second corruption is the noun eating the verb. A present is a gift. Romans 12:1 is present your bodies a living sacrifice. That is not a wrapped box and not a brand of generosity. Mercies of God first; then the body on the altar.

The third corruption is the cult of now. Webster's present tense can state what is always true. The age uses 'the present' to refuse both memory of the cross and the coming judgment. The hour is real. It is not a god.

usage: Present your bodies a living sacrifice — mercies first, then the altar (Romans 12:1).
He spoke these things while being present with you (John 14:25).
Keep being-here and setting-before as two senses; a wrapped gift is the noun, not Romans 12.

etymology: Webster 1828 prints READY (red'y) as adjective: quick; prepared; willing; at the point; easy. He cites Psalms 45:1, Matthew 22:4, Mark 14, Acts 21:13, Deuteronomy 26:5, Numbers 32:17. Companion pages already treat hope, faith, and gospel. This page fills the lookup-word men actually type when they mean prepared — not a synonym dump of prepare.
biblical_def: Ready in Scripture is not a hustle setting and not a mood of having arrived. It is prepared, willing, furnished, or at the point — under a command. Peter binds the church: always be ready to give a defense to everyone who asks you a reason for the hope that is in you, with meekness and fear. Paul says, I am ready not only to be bound, but also to die at Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus. The wedding servant says, all things are ready. Come. The dictionary therefore keeps ready from becoming a calendar excuse. The gospel is ready. The man who waits to feel ready is often only unwilling.
webster_summary: Webster 1828: READY, adjective — quick; prompt; prepared; willing; at the point; easy. He cites Matthew 22:4 (all things are ready), Mark 14 (the spirit is ready), Acts 21:13 (I am ready to die).
webster_full: READY, adjective red'y.
1. Quick; prompt; not hesitating; as ready wit; a ready consent.
5. Prepared; fitted; furnished with what is necessary. My oxen and fatlings are killed, and all things are ready. Matthew 22:4.

6. Willing; free; cheerful to do or suffer; not backward or reluctant. The spirit is ready but the flesh is weak. Mark 14:15. I am ready not to be bound only, but also to die at Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus. Acts 21:13.
8. Being at the point; near; not distant; about to do or suffer.
READY, adverb In a state of preparation, so as to need no delay. We ourselves will go ready armed before the house of Israel. Numbers 32:17.
scriptures: 1 Peter 3:15
But sanctify the Lord God in your hearts, and always be ready to give a defense to everyone who asks you a reason for the hope that is in you, with meekness and fear;
Acts 21:13
Then Paul answered, “What do you mean by weeping and breaking my heart? For I am ready not only to be bound, but also to die at Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus.”
corruption_summary: Ready is corrupted when obedience waits on a feeling, when hustle sells 'always on' as holiness, and when the wedding word 'all things are ready' is treated as an optional RSVP.
corruption_paragraphs: The first corruption is delay baptized as wisdom. 'I'll obey when I'm ready' is often unbelief with a planner. Acts 21:13 is Paul ready to be bound and to die. The name of the Lord Jesus did not wait on his comfort.
The second corruption is hustle. Always-on branding steals Peter's always be ready and strips the meekness and fear. 1 Peter 3:15 is a defense of hope, not a personal brand.
The third corruption is the feast treated as a maybe. Webster cites Matthew 22:4: all things are ready. Come. The age RSVPs the gospel as if the oxen were a vibe and the invitation a newsletter.
roots_summary: Webster 1828 prints READY with an English/Germanic family note (rid, ride, read) and no Strong's number on the fetched page. Verse-cache on the quotations below carries BTE NKJV text only. This page does not mint a Strong's number.
roots_lines: Webster 1828: READY (red'y); family note to rid / ride / read. No Strong's number printed. None invented.

Matthew 22:4 is in Webster's own citation (all things are ready). This page does not mint a Greek tag on English ready.
usage: Always be ready to give a defense of the hope in you, with meekness and fear (1 Peter 3:15).
Paul: I am ready not only to be bound, but also to die for the name of the Lord Jesus (Acts 21:13).
Do not wait to feel ready when the feast has already said, all things are ready.

etymology: Webster 1828 prints RICH from Latin rego / regnum, English reach, region: wealthy; splendid; abundant; fertile; and, in Scripture, abounding in spiritual gifts, or self-righteous in one's own opinion. He cites Genesis 13:2, James 2:5, Matthew 19:23, Revelation 3:17, Ephesians 2:4. Companion pages already treat poor, wealth, and mammon.
biblical_def: Rich in Scripture is not a brand of blessing and not a slur against industry. It is possessing much — goods, land, honor, or, by God's own mouth, faith. James asks, Has God not chosen the poor of this world to be rich in faith and heirs of the kingdom. Paul says of Christ, though He was rich, yet for your sakes He became poor, that you through His poverty might become rich. Abram was very rich in cattle, in silver and in gold — and that sentence does not make silver into election. The dictionary therefore keeps rich from becoming either a prosperity sacrament or a Marxist curse. God is rich in mercy. A man may be rich in goods and poor toward God.
webster_summary: Webster 1828: RICH, adjective — wealthy; splendid; abundant; fertile. In Scripture: abounding with spiritual gifts (James 2:5); placing confidence in outward prosperity (Matthew 19:23); self-righteous (Revelation 3:17). God is rich in mercy (Ephesians 2:4).
webster_full: RICH, adjective [Latin rego, regnum, Eng. reach, region, from extending.]
1. Wealthy; opulent; possessing a large portion of land, goods or money. Abram was very rich in cattle, in silver and in gold. Genesis 13:2.
19. In Scripture, abounding; highly endowed with spiritual gifts; as rich in faith. James 2:5.
20. Placing confidence in outward prosperity. Matthew 19:23.
21. Self-righteous; abounding, in one's own opinion, with spiritual graces. Revelation 3:17.
RICH in mercy, spoken of God, full of mercy, and ready to bestow good things on sinful men. Ephesians 2:4. Romans 10:12.
The rich used as a noun, denotes a rich man or person. The rich hath many friends. Proverbs 14:20.
scriptures: James 2:5
Listen, my beloved brethren: Has God not chosen the poor of this world to be rich in faith and heirs of the kingdom which He promised to those who love Him?
2 Corinthians 8:9
For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though He was rich, yet for your sakes He became poor, that you through His poverty might become rich.
corruption_summary: Rich is corrupted when mammon is preached as proof of election, when 'rich in faith' is inverted into a wealth seminar, and when Laodicea’s 'I am rich' is sold as healthy self-regard.
corruption_paragraphs: The first corruption is prosperity as sacrament. Webster already flagged Matthew 19:23: placing confidence in outward prosperity. The age calls that confidence 'favor.' James 2:5 is God choosing the poor of this world to be rich in faith — not poor-shaming and not a pyramid.

The second corruption is Christ's poverty as a fundraising story. 2 Corinthians 8:9 is grace: He was rich, He became poor, that you through His poverty might become rich. That richness is in Him, not in a seed-faith invoice.

The third corruption is Laodicean self-talk. Webster's sense 21 is self-righteous; abounding in one's own opinion (Revelation 3:17). 'I am rich' without need of Christ is not wellness. It is blindness.

Webster himself cites James 2:5, Matthew 19:23, Revelation 3:17, and Ephesians 2:4 on this English lemma. No Hebrew or Greek tag is minted here.
usage: God has chosen the poor of this world to be rich in faith and heirs of the kingdom (James 2:5).
Christ was rich, became poor, that you through His poverty might become rich (2 Corinthians 8:9).
Call goods goods, and faith faith; do not preach a bank balance as election.

etymology: Webster 1828 prints three English stocks in one spelling: MEAN adjective (low, base, humble), MEAN adjective/noun (middle, medium, instrument — means), and MEAN verb (to intend, purpose, signify; preterit meant). This page keeps two longer senses: to intend/signify, and low/base. The instrument sense (means of grace, by this means) is named, not mashed. Companion pages already treat purpose, good, and evil.
biblical_def:
Mean is one spelling with two honest senses. Do not mash them.

1. To intend; to signify. To mean is to have in mind, to purpose, to indicate. Joseph says, you meant evil against me; but God meant it for good, in order to save many people alive. Jesus says, go and learn what this means: I desire mercy and not sacrifice. Meaning is not a private mood. God means what He says, and He means what He does.

2. Low, base, humble in rank or worth. Mean as adjective is wanting dignity, or of little earthly value. Scripture can speak of mean things God uses, and of men who prove mean in the base sense. That is not the verb in Genesis 50. The dictionary therefore keeps mean from becoming 'what it means to me.' The text means. You submit.
webster_summary: Webster 1828: MEAN, verb — to intend; to purpose; to signify (Exodus 12:26; Genesis 50; Matthew 9:13). MEAN, adjective — low in rank; base; of little value. A second adjective/noun is the middle or instrument (means).
webster_full: MEAN, verb transitive preterit tense and participle passive meant.
1. To have in the mind, view or contemplation; to intend. What mean you by this service? Exodus 12:26.
2. To intend; to purpose; to design, with reference to a future act. Ye thought evil against me, but God meant it for good. Genesis 50.
3. To signify; to indicate. Go ye, and learn what that meaneth-- Matthew 9:13.
MEAN, adjective [Latin communis, vulgus, minor and minuo.]
1. Wanting dignity; low in rank or birth.
2. Wanting dignity of mind; low minded; base; destitute of honor; spiritless.
4. Of little value; low in worth or estimation.
MEAN, noun The middle point or place; mediocrity; medium. Also: instrument; that which is used to effect an object. Means, in the plural, income or resources.
scriptures: Genesis 50:20
But as for you, you meant evil against me; but God meant it for good, in order to bring it about as it is this day, to save many people alive.
Matthew 9:13
But go and learn what this means: ‘I desire mercy and not sacrifice.’ For I did not come to call the righteous, but sinners, to repentance.
corruption_summary: Mean is corrupted when 'what it means to me' replaces what the text means, when providence is flattened to luck, and when 'mean' as unkind swallows both the verb and the low/base adjective.
corruption_paragraphs: The first corruption is reader-response as lord. Matthew 9:13 is go and learn what this means — I desire mercy and not sacrifice. The age asks a circle, 'What does this mean to you?' as if meaning were a diary. Jesus sends them to learn.

The second corruption is providence as accident. Genesis 50:20 is two meanings in one history: you meant evil; God meant it for good. Therapy talk that treats intent as the only moral fact, and fatalism that treats God as a shrug, both refuse Joseph's sentence.

The third corruption is playground English. 'Don't be mean' is a real warning about cruelty. It is not Genesis 50 and not Matthew 9. Keep the verb, the base adjective, and the instrument (means) from eating one another.

roots_lines: Webster 1828: MEAN verb (Latin mens; Eng. mind); MEAN adjective low (Latin communis, minor); MEAN middle/instrument (Latin medium). No Strong's number printed. None invented.
Genesis 50:20 and Matthew 9:13 are BTE NKJV, fetched this hop, linked to the MBE reader.
Webster himself cites Genesis 50 and Matthew 9:13 on the verb. This page does not mint a Hebrew or Greek tag on English mean.
usage: You meant evil against me; but God meant it for good (Genesis 50:20).
Go and learn what this means: I desire mercy and not sacrifice (Matthew 9:13).
Ask what the text means, not what it means to your feed.

etymology: Webster 1828 prints CHOOSE, verb transitive: to pick out; to take by preference; to elect for eternal happiness; to elect to office. He cites Numbers 16:7, Job 34:4, Proverbs 3:31, Matthew 20, Mark 13. Companion pages already treat election, elect, and predestination. This page is the common verb men type; it is not a second election essay.
biblical_def: Choose in Scripture is to take one thing and leave another — under God's right to choose first. Jesus says to the apostles, You did not choose Me, but I chose you and appointed you that you should go and bear fruit. Moses sets life and death before Israel and commands, therefore choose life. Both sentences stand. The creature is commanded to choose; the Son is not a product the creature discovered. The dictionary therefore keeps choose from becoming a consumer sacrament. God chooses. Men answer. Fruit remains because He appointed it, not because a man branded a preference.
webster_summary: Webster 1828: CHOOSE, verb transitive — to pick out; to take by preference; to elect for eternal happiness (Many are called but few chosen); to elect to office. CHOOSE, verb intransitive — to prefer; to have the power of choice.
webster_full: CHOOSE, verb transitive
1. To pick out; to select; to take by way of preference from two or more things offered; to make choice of. The man the Lord doth choose shall be holy. Numbers 16:7.
2. To take in preference. Let us choose to us judgment. Job 34:4.
3. To prefer; to choose for imitation; to follow. Envy not the oppressor, and choose none of his ways. Proverbs 3:31.
4. To elect for eternal happiness; to predestinate to life. Many are called but few chosen. Matthew 20. For his elects sake, whom he hath chosen. Mark 13.
5. To elect or designate to office or employment by votes or suffrages.
CHOOSE, verb intransitive
1. To prefer; as, I choose to go.
2. To have the power of choice. The phrase, he cannot choose but stay, denotes that he has not the power of choice.
scriptures: John 15:16
You did not choose Me, but I chose you and appointed you that you should go and bear fruit, and that your fruit should remain, that whatever you ask the Father in My name He may give you.
Deuteronomy 30:19
I call heaven and earth as witnesses today against you, that I have set before you life and death, blessing and cursing; therefore choose life, that both you and your descendants may live;
corruption_summary: Choose is corrupted when 'I chose Jesus' reverses John 15:16, when life-and-death is recast as a lifestyle option, and when choice itself is worshiped as the last remaining virtue.
corruption_paragraphs: The first corruption is the inverted gospel. John 15:16 is You did not choose Me, but I chose you. Testimony culture that starts with the shopper's decision as the saving act has reversed the sentence. Appointment and remaining fruit are His.
The second corruption is Deuteronomy as a catalog. Choose life is a covenant command with heaven and earth as witnesses, not a brand of wellness. Death is still on the other side of the word.

The third corruption is choice as god. The age catechizes, 'You always have a choice,' as if autonomy were holiness. Webster still had elect for eternal happiness as God's act (sense 4). A ballot is not that election.
roots_summary: Webster 1828 prints the English lemma CHOOSE with no Hebrew or Greek number on the fetched page. Verse-cache on the quotations below carries BTE NKJV text only. This page does not mint a Strong's number.
roots_lines: Webster 1828: CHOOSE verb transitive and intransitive as fetched this tick. No Strong's number printed. None invented.
John 15:16 and Deuteronomy 30:19 are BTE NKJV, fetched this hop, linked to the MBE reader.
Webster's sense 4 (elect for eternal happiness) is English theology on this lemma, not a minted Strong's tag. Election / elect / predestination are companion pages.
usage: You did not choose Me, but I chose you and appointed you to bear fruit (John 15:16).
I have set before you life and death; therefore choose life (Deuteronomy 30:19).
Keep the command to choose, and keep the Son as the One who chose first.

etymology: Webster 1828 prints INHER'IT from Latin heres, an heir: to take by descent; to receive by nature from a progenitor; to possess by gift or divine appropriation. He cites Deuteronomy 16:20, Matthew 5:5, Judges 11:2. Companion pages already treat heir, promise, and covenant.
biblical_def: Inherit in Scripture is to receive as a rightful possession — by descent, by promise, or by the Lord's gift — not to seize as a wage. Jesus says, Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth. He also says that those who have left houses and lands for His name's sake shall inherit eternal life. An heir does not vote himself into the estate. The meek do not conquer the earth by branding. The dictionary therefore keeps inherit from becoming a real-estate gospel or a blood-magic of faith. God gives. The meek receive. Eternal life is inherited, not invoiced.
webster_summary: Webster 1828: INHER'IT, verb transitive — to take by descent; to receive by nature from a progenitor; to possess by gift or divine appropriation (the meek shall inherit the earth, Matthew 5:5).
webster_full: INHER'IT, verb transitive [Latin heres, an heir. See Heir.]
1. To take by descent from an ancestor; to take by succession, as the representative of the former possessor; to receive, as a right or title descendible by law from an ancestor at his decease.
2. To receive by nature from a progenitor. The son inherits the virtues of his father; children often inherit the constitutional infirmities of their parents.

3. To possess; to enjoy; to take as a possession, by gift or divine appropriation; as, to inherit everlasting life; to inherit the promises. That thou mayest live, and inherit the land which Jehovah thy God giveth thee. Deuteronomy 16:20. The meek shall inherit the earth. Matthew 5:5.
INHER'IT, verb intransitive To take or have possession or property. Thou shall not inherit in our father's house. Judges 11:2.
scriptures: Matthew 5:5
Blessed are the meek, For they shall inherit the earth.
Matthew 19:29
And everyone who has left houses or brothers or sisters or father or mother or wife or children or lands, for My name’s sake, shall receive a hundredfold, and inherit eternal life.
corruption_summary: Inherit is corrupted when the meek inheriting the earth is recast as a land-flip, when faith is treated as a blood trait, and when eternal life is talked as a wage the ambitious collect.
corruption_paragraphs: The first corruption is the real-estate beatitude. Matthew 5:5 is the meek shall inherit the earth. Dominion-by-branding and prosperity land-promises both refuse meekness. Webster's sense 3 is gift or divine appropriation, not a closing date.

The second corruption is faith as pedigree. Webster's sense 2 is receiving by nature from a progenitor — virtues and infirmities. That is not the new birth. A child may inherit a temper. He does not inherit justifying faith as a family antique.

The third corruption is eternal life as compensation. Matthew 19:29 is inherit eternal life after leaving houses and lands for His name's sake. The leaving is loss in the world. The inheriting is gift. It is not a hustle with a delayed payout chart.
roots_summary: Webster 1828 prints Latin heres (heir) on INHERIT, with no Strong's number on the fetched page. Verse-cache on the quotations below carries BTE NKJV text only. This page does not mint a Strong's number.
roots_lines: Webster 1828: Latin heres, an heir. No Strong's number printed. None invented.
Matthew 5:5 and Matthew 19:29 are BTE NKJV, fetched this hop, linked to the MBE reader.
Webster himself cites Matthew 5:5 on this English lemma. Companion pages heir / promise / covenant carry the doctrine. No Greek tag is minted here.
usage: Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth (Matthew 5:5).
Leave for His name's sake, and inherit eternal life (Matthew 19:29).
Heirs receive. They do not invoice the Father, and they do not flip the beatitude into acreage.
